paper.title_en: Towards detection of Breit-Wheeler tunnelling positrons in E320 at the FACET-II accelerator
paper.abstract_en: The SLAC Experiment 320 collides 10 TW-class laser pulses with the high-quality, 10 GeV electron beam from the FACET-II RF LINAC. This setup is expected to produce a sizable number of <math altimg="si1.svg" display="inline" id="d1e243"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> pairs via the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler mechanism in the strong-field tunnelling regime, with an estimated yield of <math altimg="si2.svg" display="inline" id="d1e261"><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow></math> pairs per collision. This small signal rate typically comes with large backgrounds, e.g., from dumping the high-charge primary beam, secondaries induced by the beam halo, as well as photons and low-energy electrons produced in the electron-laser collision itself. These backgrounds may reach densities of <math altimg="si3.svg" display="inline" id="d1e273"><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi></math>(100) charged particles per cm<sup loc="post">2</sup> (and even more neutral particles) at the surfaces of the sensing elements, making unambiguous detection of single particles a tremendous challenge. In this proceeding, we demonstrate how detectors (radiation-hard pixel detectors) and methods (particle-tracking algorithms) adapted from high-energy physics experiments can enable this measurement. We will also discuss briefly the data campaigns with our prototype detector, installed at the FACET-II tunnel in Aug 2024. We demonstrate that starting with <math altimg="si4.svg" display="inline" id="d1e283"><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></math> pixels/sensor/shot with resulting from the electron beam hitting a thin (<math altimg="si5.svg" display="inline" id="d1e292"><mrow><mn>50</mn><mspace class="nbsp" width="0.33em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow></math>) Beryllium foil (positioned next to the E320 interaction point, IP) and only <math altimg="si6.svg" display="inline" id="d1e303"><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>10</mn><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">−</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math> without this foil, we can reconstruct a signal rate of <math altimg="si7.svg" display="inline" id="d1e316"><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math> positron-like tracks per shot with the foil, or <math altimg="si8.svg" display="inline" id="d1e324"><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> without it. •SF-QED Experiment.•Focus on measuring the rate of Breit-Wheeler positrons.•Use of radiation-hard ALPIDE pixel chips.•A brief description of Experiment 320 (E320).•Particle tracking algorithm.
